The encoding scheme we propose consists of three parts. The Initialisation step is for initializing counters and state variables.
Step 1 describes the process of re-transmitting symbols $c_i$ until they have been received correctly. Step 2 is just used to fill potentially unused symbols within the block with zero symbols.
The state variables $i$ and $k$ are only updated in Step 1.

\textbf{Initialisation:} Let $i\gets 0$, $j\gets 0$, $k\gets 0$, $\boldsymbol{z}\gets(\;)$, and $\hat {\boldsymbol{y}}\gets(\;)$.

\textbf{Step 1:}  Define and transmit $e_{j+1}(m,\boldsymbol{z})=c_{i+1}(m, \hat {\boldsymbol{y}})$. Update $j\gets j+1$. Let $z_j$ be the received symbol. Update $\boldsymbol{z} \gets (\boldsymbol{z}||z_j)$. If $z_j\neq e_j(m,\boldsymbol{z})$, then repeat Step 1. Otherwise, update $i\gets i+1$, define $\boldsymbol{y}_i\gets \boldsymbol{z}_{[k+1,j]}$, update $\hat {\boldsymbol{y}}\gets (\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_i)$ and $k\gets j$. If $i=n$, then go to Step 2.  Otherwise, repeat Step 1. 

\textbf{Step 2:} If $j=n+t$, update $\boldsymbol{y}_{n}\gets(\boldsymbol{y}_n||\boldsymbol{z}_{[k+1,n+t]})$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}\gets(\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_n)$ and exit algorithm.  Otherwise, define and transmit $e_{j+1}(m,\boldsymbol{z})=0$. Update $j\gets j+1$. Let $z_j$ be the received symbol. Update $\boldsymbol{z}\gets (\boldsymbol{z}||z_j)$. Repeat Step 2.


The encoding algorithm successfully terminates after $n+t$ transmissions because we will have $n$ correct receptions within a block of $n+t$ symbols. 
The decoding scheme can just be taken from the insertion-deletion code because the output string $\boldsymbol{z}$ is a possible output of the insertion-deletion channel with at most $t$ errors for encoding functions $c_i$, $i\in [n]$. Indeed, if we define $\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{(i)}:=(\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_{i})$, we obtain
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Delta(c_i(m,\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{(i)}), \boldsymbol{y}_i)= \sum_{i=1}^{n}(|\boldsymbol{y}_i|-1)= \sum_{i=1}^{n}|\boldsymbol{y}_i| - n =(n+t)-n=t.
$$

Let $\boldsymbol{y}=(\boldsymbol{y}_1||\ldots||\boldsymbol{y}_n)=(y_1,\ldots,y_{n'})$ be a possible output string of length $n'\in[n-t,n+t]$ if the algorithm $\mathfrak{A}_{id}(M,n,\alpha)$ is used for transmitting a message $m\in[M]$ over the adversarial insertion-deletion channel with at most $t$ errors. Now we show that this string $\boldsymbol{y}$  is also a possible output if the algorithm $\mathfrak{A}_{s}(M,n',\alpha)$ is used for transmitting the same message $m\in[M]$ over the adversarial substitution channel with at most $t':=\lfloor (n' - n+t) /2 \rfloor$ errors.  Define $\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{(i-1)}:=(\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1})\in\left(\{0,1\}^*\right)^{i-1}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}^{(i-1)}:=(y_1,\ldots,y_{i-1})\in\{0,1\}^{i-1}$. Let $c_i=c_i(m,\hat {\boldsymbol{y}}^{(i-1)})$ and $e_i=e_i(m,\boldsymbol{y}^{(i-1)})$ be the $i$th bit generated by the encoders of the feedback insertion-deletion code and the substitution code, respectively. We define $\boldsymbol{e}:=(e_1,\ldots,e_{n'})$. So, it suffices to show that $d_H(\boldsymbol{e},\boldsymbol{y})\le t'$.  Denote the length of $\boldsymbol{y}_i$ by $n_i$. We represent $\boldsymbol{e}$ as the concatenation $(\boldsymbol{e}_1||\ldots||\boldsymbol{e}_n)$ such that the binary string $\boldsymbol{e}_i$ has length $n_i$. It is clear that for ``synchronized" moments $i$ and $N_i:=n_1+\dots+n_{i-1}+1$, both algorithms send the same symbol, i.e., 
$$
c_{i}(m,\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{(i-1)})=e_{N_i}(m,\boldsymbol{y}^{(N_i-1)}).
$$
By the definition of the algorithm, it can be readily checked that if $y_j\neq e_j$, then $e_{j+1}=e_j$, i.e., a re-transmission occurs.
Therefore, 
$$
d_H(\boldsymbol{e}_{i},\boldsymbol{y}_{i})\le 
\begin{cases}
n_{i} -1, &\text{if }\Delta(c_{i}, \boldsymbol{y}_{i})= n_{i}-1,\\
n_{i},&\text{if }\Delta(c_{i}, \boldsymbol{y}_{i})= n_{i}+1.
\end{cases}
$$
Note that the second case can only happen when a deletion occurred. Let $t_{ins}$ be the total number of insertions and $t_{del}$ be the total number of deletions. 
We have the restrictions $t_{ins}+t_{del}\le t$ and $n-t_{del}+t_{ins} = n'$. This implies that
$n' - n + 2 t_{del} \le t$ or $t_{del} \le \lfloor(n-n' + t)/2 \rfloor$. It follows that 
$$
d_H(\boldsymbol{e},\boldsymbol{y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}d_H(\boldsymbol{e}_{i},\boldsymbol{y}_{i})\le \sum_{i=1}^{n} n_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}\{\Delta(c_{i}, \boldsymbol{y}_{i})=n_i-1\} \le n' - (n-t_{del})  \le t',
$$
where $\mathbb{1}\{x=a\}$ denotes the indicator function of the event $x=a$.

    According to Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent_hamming} by fixing $\alpha=2\tau / (1+\tau)$ and using the algorithm $\mathfrak{A}_s(M,n',\alpha)$ for $n' = \lfloor n(1+\tau)\rfloor - 2k$ and at most $\lfloor \tau n \rfloor - k$ errors the achievable rates form the tangent line to the point $(\tau/(1+\tau),R_s(\tau/(1+\tau)))$ of the function $R_s(x)=1-h(x)$.
    
    To prove the required claim concerning the minimization, we define the function

        f(x): = \frac{\log M_s(n(1+\tau-2x), (\tau-x)n,\alpha)}{n} = (1+\tau-2x) \left(a \frac{\tau-x}{1+\tau-2x}+b\right)(1+o(1)),

    A short computation shows that $a = \log\tau$ and $b = 1-\log(1+\tau)$.
    
    The derivative of $f(x)$ as $n\to\infty$ is
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = -a - 2b + o(1) = \log\left(\frac{(1+\tau)^2}{\tau}\right)  -2 + o(1) > 0,
    \end{equation*}
    where the inequality follows the argument of the logarithm is strictly greater than $4$ for $\tau<1/2$.
